topics.name: Plasma (physics)
topics.kicker: The fourth state of matter · Glowing gas of ions and free electrons
topics.briefing: Heat a gas enough, or zap it with electricity, and its atoms lose electrons, leaving a glowing soup of free electrons and charged ions called plasma. It is often called the fourth state of matter, after solid, liquid, and gas. Lightning, the glow inside neon signs, and the Sun are all plasma, and most of the ordinary matter in the universe is in this state.
topics.answerHtml: Plasma (prompt on ionized gas; do not accept “blood plasma”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Irving Langmuir [“LANG-myoor”] gave this state of matter its name in 1928, reportedly comparing it to the liquid part of blood that carries blood cells. Probes named for Langmuir measure the electron temperature and density of this state of matter.
tossups.r: Lightning and the Sun are made of it. For 10 points, name this state of matter, a hot gas of charged ions and free electrons.

tossups.p: William Crookes called this state of matter “radiant matter” in 1879 while studying the glowing gas inside his cathode-ray tubes. In this state, a gas has been heated or energized so much that electrons are stripped from its atoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fourth state of matter, found in lightning, neon signs, and stars.

tossups.p: In this state of matter, free charges gather around any extra charge and cancel out its electric field beyond a distance called the Debye [“deh-BYE”] length. As a whole, this state of matter is almost exactly electrically neutral, since it holds equal amounts of positive and negative charge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter made of ions and free electrons, which makes up the Sun.

tossups.p: Hannes Alfvén [“al-VAIN”] won the 1970 Nobel Prize in Physics for magnetohydrodynamics, which treats this state of matter as an electrically conducting fluid, and waves in it are named for him. Magnetic fields can trap this state of matter because its charged particles spiral around field lines.
tossups.r: It is often called the fourth state of matter. For 10 points, name this state of matter found in neon signs and the Sun.

tossups.p: Sailors in thunderstorms sometimes saw a blue glow called St. Elmo’s fire on their ships’ masts, made when a strong electric field turns the air into this state of matter. Novelty glass-globe lamps send glowing streamers of it toward any finger touching the glass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, an ionized gas found in lightning and stars.

tossups.p: Radio waves below a natural oscillation frequency of this state of matter bounce off it, which is why AM radio signals can reflect off the ionosphere and travel far beyond the horizon at night. Electrons in this state of matter can slosh back and forth in Langmuir waves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, often called the fourth state after solid, liquid, and gas.

tossups.p: In a Z-pinch, an electric current flowing through this state of matter creates a magnetic field that squeezes it inward. Tokamaks use powerful magnets to hold this state of matter at over 100 million degrees so that nuclear fusion can happen.
tossups.r: Lightning bolts are made of it. For 10 points, name this state of matter made of ions and free electrons.

tossups.p: Until about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the whole universe was filled with this state of matter, which blocked light; when it cooled into neutral atoms, the light that became the cosmic microwave background was set free.
tossups.r: Neon signs glow because the gas inside them is turned into this state of matter. For 10 points, name this fourth state of matter.

tossups.p: The Sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona, is made of this state of matter at more than a million degrees, and a stream of it flowing outward is called the solar wind. When that stream hits Earth’s magnetic field, it helps produce the northern and southern lights.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, made when a gas gets so hot that electrons are torn from its atoms.

tossups.p: Computer chip factories use this state of matter to etch tiny patterns into silicon wafers, and metalworkers use torches of it to cut through steel. Fluorescent tubes glow when the mercury vapor inside them becomes this state of matter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fourth state of matter, made of ions and free electrons.

tossups.p: A lightning bolt heats the air in its channel to around 30,000 kelvins, about five times hotter than the Sun’s surface, turning the air into this state of matter. The sudden expansion of that superheated air makes thunder.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, an ionized gas that also makes up the stars.

tossups.p: Solar flares happen when tangled magnetic field lines in the Sun’s atmosphere suddenly snap and reconnect, releasing energy into this state of matter. Because it is full of free charges, this state of matter conducts electricity very well, unlike an ordinary gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, which makes up the Sun and lightning.

tossups.p: Some older flat-screen TVs lit up millions of tiny cells of xenon and neon gas by turning them into this state of matter. Each kind of gas glows its own color in this state, which is why a neon sign shines red-orange.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, a gas whose atoms have lost some of their electrons.

tossups.p: A spacecraft plunging back into the atmosphere heats the air around it into a glowing sheath of this state of matter, which can briefly block radio signals. Magnetic fields can steer this state of matter, since its charged particles spiral around magnetic field lines.
tossups.r: Most of the ordinary matter in the universe is in this state. For 10 points, name this state of matter made of ions and free electrons, found inside glowing neon signs.

tossups.p: A comet’s straight, bluish ion tail is made of this state of matter and is pushed directly away from the Sun by the solar wind. In this state, many electrons have broken free of their atoms.
tossups.r: Lightning and the stars are made of it. For 10 points, name this fourth state of matter, after solid, liquid, and gas.

trap.title: Physics plasma, not blood
trap.body: Biology tossups also use the word: blood plasma is the yellowish liquid part of blood, and a cell’s plasma membrane is a different answer line again. In physics, the other states of matter are traps too: a Bose–Einstein condensate is an ultracold state, the opposite extreme from this superhot one.
trap.fix: Ions, free electrons, lightning, stars, tokamaks, auroras, Langmuir, and Crookes’s “radiant matter” mean plasma, the state of matter. Red and white blood cells, platelets, and clotting mean blood plasma; atoms chilled to near absolute zero mean a Bose–Einstein condensate.
trap.line: Real answer line: Plasma (prompt on ionized gas; do not accept “blood plasma”)

topics.name: Temperature
topics.kicker: How hot or cold something is · Measured in kelvins, °C, or °F
topics.briefing: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is, and deep down it measures how fast the atoms and molecules inside are jiggling around. Scientists measure it in kelvins, where zero is absolute zero, the coldest anything can possibly get, while weather reports use degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit. Heat always flows on its own from a place of higher temperature to one of lower temperature, never the other way.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In thermodynamics, the reciprocal of this quantity equals how fast a system’s entropy rises as energy is added to it. The equipartition theorem says each independent way a gas molecule can move or spin gets an average energy of one-half Boltzmann’s constant times this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity measured by a thermometer, which tells how hot or cold something is.

tossups.p: When Anders Celsius made his scale for this quantity in 1742, he put 0 at water’s boiling point and 100 at its freezing point, the reverse of the modern version. His scale was widely called “centigrade” until an international conference renamed it in 1948.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that measures how hot or cold something is, often read off a thermometer.

tossups.p: The old Réaumur [“RAY-oh-myoor”] scale for this quantity put water’s boiling point at 80 degrees. The Rankine [“RANG-kin”] scale starts at absolute zero like the Kelvin scale, but its degrees are the same size as Fahrenheit degrees.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that a thermometer measures, telling how hot or cold something is.

tossups.p: In the 1590s, Galileo built a thermoscope, an air-filled glass bulb whose tube dipped into water, which showed changes in this quantity but had no numbered scale. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit later made the first reliable mercury thermometer, in 1714.
tossups.r: On his scale, water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212. For 10 points, name this quantity measured by thermometers.

tossups.p: Ralph Fowler named the zeroth law of thermodynamics, which says that if two objects are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they share the same value of this quantity. That law is what makes thermometers work.
tossups.r: Heat flows on its own from an object where this quantity is higher to one where it is lower. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in kelvins.

tossups.p: Since 2019, the SI unit of this quantity has been defined by fixing the exact value of the Boltzmann constant; before that, it was defined using the triple point of water, set at exactly 273.16 of those units.
tossups.r: That unit is the kelvin, one of the seven SI base units. For 10 points, name this quantity, which measures how hot or cold something is.

tossups.p: In 1821, Thomas Seebeck [“ZAY-bek”] noticed that a loop made of two different metals deflected a compass needle when one of its junctions was heated, an effect that thermocouples use to measure this quantity. A bimetallic strip in an old thermostat bends when this quantity changes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that a thermometer measures, given in degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit.

tossups.p: According to Wien’s [“VEENZ”] displacement law, the peak wavelength of light given off by a glowing object, like a star or a stove burner, is inversely proportional to this quantity, which is why blue stars are hotter than red ones.
tossups.r: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots it, increasing to the left. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in kelvins.

tossups.p: The Stefan–Boltzmann law says the energy a glowing object radiates each second rises with the fourth power of this quantity measured in kelvins, so doubling it makes the object give off 16 times as much energy. Pyrometers measure this quantity in furnaces from a distance.
tossups.r: Fever thermometers measure it. For 10 points, name this quantity that tells how hot something is.

tossups.p: The cosmic microwave background left over from the Big Bang has a value of this quantity of about 2.7 kelvins, as measured precisely by the COBE [“KOH-bee”] satellite. The Boomerang Nebula, at about 1 kelvin, is the coldest known natural place in the universe.
tossups.r: Thermometers measure it. For 10 points, name this quantity given in kelvins, degrees Celsius, or degrees Fahrenheit.

tossups.p: Gay-Lussac’s [“gay-loo-SAKS”] law says the pressure of a gas in a sealed, rigid container rises in proportion to this quantity, while Charles’s law says a gas’s volume at constant pressure does the same. In the ideal gas law, P V equals n R times this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity measured by a thermometer, which tells how hot or cold something is.

tossups.p: In 1868, the German doctor Carl Wunderlich [“VOON-der-lish”] studied many thousands of patients and set the normal value of this quantity for the human body at about 37 degrees Celsius. Nurses check it with oral, ear, or forehead thermometers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, traditionally about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit for a healthy person.

tossups.p: Negative 40 is the one reading where the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales for this quantity agree. To convert a reading of this quantity from Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by nine-fifths and then add 32.
tossups.r: Water boils at 212 degrees on the Fahrenheit scale for this quantity. For 10 points, name this measure of how hot or cold something is.

tossups.p: In the troposphere, this quantity drops by about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometer you climb, a change called the lapse rate, but it rises again in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs ultraviolet light.
tossups.r: Wind chill and the heat index describe how this quantity feels to people. For 10 points, name this quantity that weather forecasters report in degrees.

tossups.p: The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, which shows how fast the molecules in a gas are moving, gets wider and shifts to higher speeds as this quantity rises. A spoonful and a whole pot of the same soup can share the same value of this quantity.
tossups.r: For an ideal gas, it is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the molecules. For 10 points, name this quantity measured in degrees or kelvins.

clues.t: Measures how hot or cold something is, using a thermometer
Measured in degrees Celsius, degrees Fahrenheit, or kelvins
Water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F) and boils at 100 °C (212 °F) at sea level
Proportional to the average kinetic energy of a gas’s particles
Heat flows on its own from where it is higher to where it is lower
The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero (−273.15 °C), the coldest possible
Lord Kelvin proposed the absolute scale in 1848; the kelvin is one of the seven SI base units
Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit made the first reliable mercury thermometer (1714)
Anders Celsius (1742) first put 0 at boiling and 100 at freezing; his scale was called “centigrade” until 1948
Negative 40 reads the same in Celsius and Fahrenheit; to convert, multiply Celsius by nine-fifths and add 32
Normal for the human body: about 37 °C (98.6 °F), set by Carl Wunderlich in 1868
Charles’s law (volume) and Gay-Lussac’s law (pressure) grow in proportion to it; PV = nRT
The zeroth law of thermodynamics (named by Ralph Fowler) is what makes thermometers work
Its reciprocal equals how fast entropy rises as energy is added (1/T = dS/dU)
Equipartition theorem: each way a gas molecule can move or spin gets an average energy of one-half k times it
Rankine scale: starts at absolute zero with Fahrenheit-sized degrees; Réaumur scale: water boils at 80
Galileo’s thermoscope (1590s) showed changes but had no numbered scale
Since 2019 the kelvin is defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant; before, by water’s triple point (273.16 K)
Thermocouples use the Seebeck effect (1821): two metals joined in a loop respond when one junction is heated
A bimetallic strip in an old thermostat bends as it changes
Wien’s law: peak wavelength is inversely proportional to it, so blue stars are hotter than red ones
Stefan–Boltzmann law: a glowing object’s radiated power grows with the fourth power of it
Pyrometers measure it in furnaces from a distance
Cosmic microwave background: about 2.7 K (measured by COBE); the Boomerang Nebula, about 1 K, is the coldest known natural place
Lapse rate: in the troposphere it drops about 6.5 °C per kilometer; it rises again in the stratosphere
The Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution widens and shifts to higher speeds as it rises
An intensive property: a spoonful and a whole pot of the same soup can share the same value

trap.title: Temperature is not heat
trap.body: Heat is energy that moves from a hotter object to a colder one; temperature measures how hot something is, the average jiggling energy of its particles. A bathtub of warm water holds more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water, even though the cup has the higher temperature. Heat capacity and absolute zero are separate answer lines too.
trap.fix: Thermometers, degrees, kelvins, Celsius, Fahrenheit, and “average kinetic energy” point to temperature. Energy transferred, joules, and calories point to heat; how much energy it takes to warm something up is heat capacity.
trap.line: Real answer line: Temperature (prompt on T; do not accept “heat”)

topics.name: Momentum
topics.kicker: Mass times velocity · Conserved when objects collide
topics.briefing: Momentum is mass in motion: multiply an object’s mass by its velocity and you get its momentum, which is why a slow-rolling bowling ball is harder to stop than a speeding ping-pong ball. In a collision, the total momentum stays the same as long as no outside force interferes. That rule explains why a skater who throws a heavy ball rolls backward, and how rockets push themselves through empty space.
topics.answerHtml: Momentum (accept linear momentum; prompt on p; do not accept “angular momentum”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his 1924 thesis, Louis de Broglie [“duh BROY”] proposed that any particle has a wavelength equal to Planck’s constant divided by this quantity. Werner Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle says that this quantity and position cannot both be known exactly at the same time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, equal to mass times velocity, that is conserved in collisions.

tossups.p: Arthur Compton won a Nobel Prize after showing in 1923 that X-ray photons bounce off electrons like billiard balls, handing over some of their energy and this quantity. In that Compton effect, the scattered X-rays come out with longer wavelengths.
tossups.r: It is conserved in collisions. For 10 points, name this quantity, equal to mass times velocity for everyday objects.

tossups.p: Emmy Noether’s [“NUR-terz”] theorem shows that the conservation of this quantity comes from the fact that the laws of physics are the same everywhere in space. Stepping off a small rowboat onto a dock pushes the boat away in the opposite direction, since the total of this quantity is conserved.
tossups.r: The total amount of it stays the same when two carts collide on a track. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized p, which equals mass times velocity.

tossups.p: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky’s [“tsee-ul-KOF-skeez”] 1903 rocket equation comes from applying the conservation of this quantity to a rocket that throws exhaust out its back. Because of that conservation law, a rocket can speed up in empty space with nothing to push against.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, mass times velocity, which is conserved in collisions.

tossups.p: Japan’s IKAROS spacecraft, launched in 2010, was the first to show that a solar sail works in interplanetary space; sunlight pushes such a sail with the tiny amount of this quantity it carries. A photon’s value of this quantity equals its energy divided by the speed of light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized p, that equals mass times velocity for ordinary objects.

tossups.p: René Descartes [“day-KART”] claimed in 1644 that the total “quantity of motion” in the universe never changes, but he ignored direction, a mistake Christiaan Huygens [“HOY-gunz”] fixed while studying collisions. This quantity is a vector, so it points in the same direction as an object’s velocity.
tossups.r: Isaac Newton also used the name “quantity of motion” for it. For 10 points, name this quantity, equal to mass times velocity.

tossups.p: Isaac Newton’s second law, in its general form, says that the net force on an object equals the rate at which this quantity changes. Airbags protect people in car crashes by stretching out the time it takes to change this quantity, which lowers the force.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, mass times velocity, which is conserved when objects collide.

tossups.p: In a Newton’s cradle, lifting and releasing one steel ball sends exactly one ball swinging out from the other end, because both this quantity and kinetic energy are conserved. Two ice skaters who push off each other glide apart with equal and opposite amounts of this quantity.
tossups.r: It is measured in kilogram meters per second. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized p, which equals mass times velocity.

tossups.p: In a perfectly inelastic collision, such as two train cars that couple together, some kinetic energy turns into heat and sound, but this quantity is still conserved. The change in this quantity equals the impulse, which is force multiplied by time.
tossups.r: A slow bowling ball can have more of it than a fast ping-pong ball. For 10 points, name this quantity, equal to mass times velocity.

tossups.p: When a moving cue ball hits a resting billiard ball of the same mass head-on, the cue ball stops dead and the other ball rolls off with all of this quantity. Unlike kinetic energy, this quantity is a vector, so equal amounts moving in opposite directions add up to zero.
tossups.r: It is measured in newton-seconds. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized p, equal to mass times velocity.

tossups.p: Physicists find a charged particle’s value of this quantity from how tightly its track curves in a magnetic field, since a larger value makes a wider curve. In special relativity, this quantity equals the Lorentz factor times mass times velocity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, mass times velocity, that is conserved when two objects collide.

tossups.p: Two equal lumps of clay thrown at each other at the same speed stick together and stop dead, because their total of this quantity was zero before they hit. Crumple zones in cars fold up during a crash, stretching out the time it takes to change this quantity so the force on passengers is smaller.
tossups.r: It is conserved in collisions. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized p, which equals mass times velocity in everyday physics.

tossups.p: When a firework shell bursts in midair, its pieces fly apart in all directions, but the total of this quantity just after the burst equals the total just before. A system’s center of mass keeps a steady velocity when this quantity is conserved.
tossups.r: A truck has more of it than a bicycle moving at the same speed. For 10 points, name this quantity, mass times velocity.

tossups.p: If the push of this quantity carried by light drove a Crookes radiometer, its vanes would spin the opposite way; instead, warm gas molecules push them. A squid jets forward by squirting water backward because this quantity is conserved.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, equal to mass times velocity, that is conserved when objects collide.

tossups.p: Newton’s third law guarantees that this quantity is conserved, because when two objects push on each other, they change each other’s amounts of it equally and oppositely. This quantity is measured in kilogram meters per second, the same units as a newton-second.
tossups.r: A charging football player is hard to stop because he has a lot of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, symbolized p, equal to mass times velocity.

clues.t: Mass times velocity (p = mv)
Conserved in collisions as long as no outside force acts
Symbolized p; measured in kilogram meters per second (the same as newton-seconds)
A heavy truck has far more than a bicycle moving at the same speed
A vector: it points in the same direction as the velocity
Impulse (force multiplied by time) equals its change
Airbags and crumple zones stretch out the time it takes to change it, which lowers the force on people in a crash
Newton’s cradle: one ball in, one ball out, conserving it along with kinetic energy
Conserved even in perfectly inelastic collisions, where some kinetic energy is lost
Newton’s second law, in its general form: net force equals its rate of change
Rockets and squids move forward by pushing exhaust or water backward
Two skaters who push off each other get equal and opposite amounts
A cue ball hitting an equal ball head-on stops and passes on all of it
Newton’s third law guarantees its conservation: pushes between two objects change their amounts equally and oppositely
Louis de Broglie (1924): a particle’s wavelength equals Planck’s constant divided by it
Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle: it and position cannot both be known exactly
Compton effect (1923): X-ray photons hand some of it to electrons and come out with longer wavelengths
Noether’s theorem: its conservation comes from the laws of physics being the same everywhere in space
Stepping off a small rowboat onto a dock pushes the boat away in the opposite direction, since its total is conserved
Konstantin Tsiolkovsky’s 1903 rocket equation comes from its conservation
Light carries it even though photons have no mass (energy divided by the speed of light), so it can push solar sails like Japan’s IKAROS (2010)
Descartes (1644) said the “quantity of motion” is conserved but ignored direction; Huygens fixed this, and Newton used the same name
Found from how tightly a charged particle’s track curves in a magnetic field
In special relativity, it equals the Lorentz factor times mass times velocity
Two equal lumps of clay thrown at each other at the same speed stick together and stop: their total was zero
A Crookes radiometer spins the opposite way from what light’s push would cause; warm gas really drives it
A bursting firework shell’s pieces have the same total just after the burst as just before

trap.title: Linear, not angular
trap.body: Momentum (mass times velocity) and angular momentum (the spinning version) are separate answer lines: “angular momentum” is wrong on a collision question, and plain “momentum” only earns a prompt on a spinning one. Players also confuse momentum with impulse, which is the change in momentum, and with kinetic energy, which is not conserved in inelastic collisions.
trap.fix: Collisions, p = mv, impulse, airbags, rockets, Newton’s cradle, and de Broglie wavelengths mean momentum. Spinning skaters, torque, orbits, Kepler’s equal areas, and L mean angular momentum. If a question asks for the quantity that an impulse changes, the answer is momentum, not impulse.
trap.line: Real answer line: Momentum (accept linear momentum; prompt on p; do not accept “angular momentum”)

topics.name: Potential energy
topics.kicker: Stored energy of position · Equals mass times g times height
topics.briefing: Potential energy is energy waiting to happen: a boulder perched on a cliff, a stretched rubber band, and a drawn bow all store it because of their position or shape. Lift something and you give it gravitational potential energy equal to its mass times g times its height; let it fall, and that energy turns into kinetic energy. The Scottish engineer William Rankine gave it its name in 1853.
topics.answerHtml: Potential energy (accept PE; accept specific types such as gravitational potential energy or elastic potential energy; prompt on energy or potential; do not accept “kinetic energy”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: William Rankine, who also names a temperature scale with Fahrenheit-sized degrees, gave this quantity its modern name in 1853. Subtracting this quantity from kinetic energy gives the Lagrangian, and a conservative force equals the negative gradient, or downhill slope, of this quantity.
tossups.r: For a raised object, this quantity equals mass times g times height. For 10 points, name this energy an object stores because of its position.

tossups.p: For gravity, this quantity is usually defined as zero at infinite separation, so it is negative at every finite distance. Carrying a box up a long ramp or straight up a ladder to the same height adds the same amount of this quantity, because only the change in height matters, not the path taken.
tossups.r: A stretched spring stores one-half k x squared of it. For 10 points, name this stored energy of position, the partner of kinetic energy.

tossups.p: A system rests in stable equilibrium wherever this quantity is at a minimum. In the pole vault, an athlete’s kinetic energy is stored in the bending pole as the elastic form of this quantity, then turned into the gravitational form as the vaulter rises over the bar.
tossups.r: A boulder perched on a cliff has a lot of it. For 10 points, name this energy stored because of an object’s position.

tossups.p: Pumped-storage power plants use spare electricity to push water uphill into a high reservoir, banking this quantity until the water flows back down through turbines. The amount of this quantity a lake behind a dam holds depends on how far the water sits above a chosen reference level.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy of position, equal to mass times g times height near Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: For many simple systems, the Hamiltonian equals kinetic energy plus this quantity, which is often written U or V. Gravity, spring forces, and electric forces each have a version of this quantity, but friction does not, because friction is not a conservative force.
tossups.r: A roller coaster has the most of it at the top of its highest hill. For 10 points, name this stored energy of position.

tossups.p: Setting an object’s kinetic energy equal to the size of this quantity lets you calculate a planet’s escape velocity. Between two masses, the gravitational form of this quantity equals negative G times the product of the masses, divided by the distance between them.
tossups.r: Near the ground, it equals m g h. For 10 points, name this energy that an object stores because of where it is.

tossups.p: Dividing the electric version of this quantity by a small test charge gives a value measured in volts. For two point charges, this quantity equals Coulomb’s constant times the product of the charges divided by the distance between them.
tossups.r: The chemical energy stored in food and fuel is a form of it. For 10 points, name this stored energy, which turns into kinetic energy as an object falls.

tossups.p: Only changes in this quantity matter physically, so physicists may choose any convenient level to call zero. In a swinging pendulum, this quantity peaks at the two ends of each swing, where the bob stops for an instant.
tossups.r: Adding it to kinetic energy gives mechanical energy. For 10 points, name this energy of position, which turns into motion when an object drops.

tossups.p: Chemists graph how this quantity changes during a reaction, and the height of the hump that rises above the reactants on that graph is the activation energy. In an exothermic reaction, the products end up with less of this quantity than the reactants had.
tossups.r: A drawn bow stores this kind of energy until the arrow is released. For 10 points, name this energy stored because of position or shape.

tossups.p: A particle trapped in a region where this quantity is low is said to sit in a “well,” as in the infinite square well of quantum mechanics. A spring stretched a distance x stores one-half k x squared of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this stored energy, also found in rubber bands, drawn bows, and objects lifted off the ground.

tossups.p: The work done on an object by a conservative force equals the negative of the change in this quantity. A ball thrown straight up trades its kinetic energy for this quantity until it reaches the top of its path.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this stored energy that a raised object has, which depends on its mass and its height.

tossups.p: In the Lagrangian of classical mechanics, written L equals T minus V, this quantity is the V. Lifting a 1-kilogram mass by 1 meter near Earth’s surface adds about 9.8 joules of this quantity.
tossups.r: Water held behind a dam and a book on a high shelf both have it. For 10 points, name this energy of position.

tossups.p: As two hydrogen atoms approach each other, this quantity falls to its lowest point at the bond length, and energy is released as the bond forms. Breaking that bond again requires adding energy to raise this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy stored in a system because of the positions of its parts, the counterpart of kinetic energy.

tossups.p: On a graph of this quantity against position, the negative of the slope at any point gives the force on an object. A pencil balanced on its tip is in unstable equilibrium because it sits at a peak of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this energy of position, which a diver on a high platform has more of than a diver on a low board.

tossups.p: Pulling apart two magnets that attract each other increases this quantity, as does separating a positive charge from a negative one. Food, fuel, and batteries store chemical energy, which is really a form of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this stored energy of position or arrangement, the partner of kinetic energy.

clues.t: Energy an object stores because of its position, shape, or arrangement
Near Earth’s surface, its gravitational form equals mass times g times height (m g h)
The partner of kinetic energy: a falling object converts it into kinetic energy
Examples: a boulder on a cliff, water behind a dam, a drawn bow, a stretched rubber band
A roller coaster has the most of it at the top of its highest hill
Its elastic form: a spring stretched or squeezed a distance x stores one-half k x squared
Added to kinetic energy, it gives mechanical energy, which stays constant when there is no friction
Only conservative forces (gravity, springs, electric forces) have a version of it; friction does not
Only changes in it matter, so physicists may choose any convenient reference level as zero
A pendulum has the most of it at the two ends of each swing and the least at the bottom
Chemical energy stored in food, fuel, and batteries is a form of it
Pumped-storage power plants push water uphill to store it, then let the water flow back down through turbines
The work done by a conservative force equals the negative of its change
Named in 1853 by Scottish engineer William Rankine, who also names a temperature scale with Fahrenheit-sized degrees
The Lagrangian is kinetic energy minus this: L equals T minus V
For many systems, the Hamiltonian (the total energy) is kinetic energy plus this
Usually given the symbol U, or V in the Lagrangian
A conservative force equals its negative gradient: on a graph against position, force is the negative of the slope
Stable equilibrium sits at a minimum of it; a pencil balanced on its tip is at a peak (unstable equilibrium)
Between two masses, its gravitational form is negative G M m over r: zero at infinite distance and negative everywhere closer
Setting kinetic energy equal to the size of its gravitational form gives a planet’s escape velocity
Between two point charges: Coulomb’s constant times the two charges over r; dividing by charge gives a value in volts
Carrying a box up a ramp or straight up a ladder to the same height adds the same amount: only the height change matters, not the path
In the pole vault, kinetic energy is stored in the bending pole as its elastic form, then turned into its gravitational form
On a graph of it during a chemical reaction, the hump rising above the reactants is the activation energy
In an exothermic reaction, the products end up with less of it than the reactants had
A particle trapped where it is low sits in a “well,” like the infinite square well of quantum mechanics

trap.title: Stored, moving, or volts?
trap.body: This is the stored half of mechanical energy; kinetic energy is the half that comes from motion, and the two are separate answers with separate pages on this site. Players also blurt out “electric potential” or “voltage,” but that is this energy divided by charge, measured in volts, so it is a different answer. A bare “energy” or “potential” only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Height, springs, position, the letters U or V, or the minus sign in the Lagrangian point here. One-half m v squared or speed means kinetic energy, and volts mean voltage. If you are prompted, say the full two words.
trap.line: Real answer line: Potential energy (accept PE or specific types such as gravitational potential energy; prompt on energy; do not accept “kinetic energy”)

topics.name: Surface tension
topics.kicker: A liquid’s stretchy skin · Lets water striders walk on ponds
topics.dates: Explained by Thomas Young and Pierre-Simon Laplace, 1805–1806
topics.briefing: Surface tension makes the top of a liquid behave like a stretchy skin. Water molecules cling to one another, so the ones at the top get pulled inward, which lets water striders skate across ponds and a carefully placed paper clip rest on water. Add a drop of dish soap and that skin weakens, so the paper clip sinks.
topics.answerHtml: Surface tension (prompt on tension; do not accept “capillary action” or “cohesion”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Agnes Pockels measured this property using a homemade trough in her kitchen, and Lord Rayleigh helped get her results published in _Nature_ in 1891. In a classic classroom experiment, students count how many drops of water they can pile onto a penny, where this property holds the water in a bulging dome until it spills.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that lets water striders walk on a pond, caused by the cohesion of water molecules.

tossups.p: The Young–Laplace equation says the pressure inside a curved drop exceeds the outside pressure by an amount that depends on this property and the drop’s radius. Because of that, the air inside a small bubble is at a higher pressure than the air inside a large one.
tossups.r: Soap lowers this property. For 10 points, name this property that makes a liquid’s top layer act like a stretched elastic skin.

tossups.p: The Marangoni [“mar-un-GOH-nee”] effect, named for an Italian physicist, makes liquid flow from places where this property is low toward places where it is high. A drop of soap behind a toy boat lowers this property there, so the boat zooms forward.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of liquids, which is unusually high for water because of hydrogen bonding.

tossups.p: James Jurin [“JOOR-in”] found that the height a liquid climbs in a thin glass tube is inversely proportional to the tube’s radius, a rise that depends directly on this property. Water’s meniscus curves upward at the glass because water molecules are attracted to the glass more strongly than to each other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that lets a paper clip float on water and makes small drops form spheres.

tossups.p: A du Noüy [“doo noo-EE”] ring can be pulled up out of a liquid to measure this property, which has units of newtons per meter. Mercury has a much higher value of this property than water, which is why spilled mercury breaks into shiny beads.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, often symbolized gamma, that lets insects called water striders stand on ponds.

tossups.p: Joseph Plateau [“plah-TOH”] found that stable soap films meet in threes at angles of 120 degrees, because this property pulls each film into the smallest possible area. The same property makes a thin falling stream of water break up into droplets.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that pulls a liquid into shapes with the least possible exposed area, such as spherical drops.

tossups.p: Tiny air sacs in the lungs called alveoli [“al-VEE-uh-lye”] are coated with a substance that lowers this property so they do not collapse. Detergents and other surfactants also lower this property, which lets water spread out and soak into fabric.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property caused by cohesion, which lets a needle rest on top of water.

tossups.p: Water ripples with wavelengths under about two centimeters are called capillary waves because this property, rather than gravity, mainly pulls them flat again. This property also pulls a soap bubble into a sphere, the shape that encloses its air with the least possible area of film.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured in newtons per meter, that makes water bead up into round drops.

tossups.p: In 1805, Thomas Young related the contact angle of a drop resting on a solid to this property, often symbolized gamma. A drop of water on a waxy leaf beads up instead of spreading because the water’s cohesion beats its attraction to the wax.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that lets water striders walk on ponds and is lowered by soap.

tossups.p: This property can be given in newtons per meter or in joules per square meter, the energy needed to make each square meter of new liquid boundary. Molecules in a liquid’s top layer have fewer neighbors above them, so they feel a net inward pull.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that makes a liquid behave as if it had a stretchy skin.

tossups.p: Soap and detergent molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail, so they crowd onto the top of water and lower this property. A glass can be filled slightly above its rim, forming a dome of water, because of this property.
tossups.r: It lets water striders skate across ponds. For 10 points, name this property that makes a liquid act as if it had a stretchy skin.

tossups.p: A drop hanging from a faucet or an eyedropper falls only when its weight grows larger than the pull of this property holding it on. This property is lowered by raising a liquid’s temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of liquids that makes a drop pull itself into a sphere and lets small insects stand on water.

tossups.p: Small raindrops are nearly perfect spheres because of this property, while large raindrops are flattened by air resistance into a hamburger-bun shape. Astronauts on the International Space Station have watched floating blobs of water pull themselves into balls thanks to this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property caused by the cohesion of liquid molecules, which soap lowers.

tossups.p: At room temperature, water’s value of this property is about 72 millinewtons per meter, higher than that of most common liquids, because hydrogen bonds hold water molecules tightly together. Raising water’s temperature or adding soap lowers this value.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that lets a carefully placed needle or paper clip rest on top of water.

tossups.p: In the “Cheerios effect,” floating bits of cereal drift together and clump, an effect caused by this property and buoyancy. Water striders rest on ponds on legs covered in tiny water-repelling hairs that dimple the water without breaking through.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of liquids, which is lowered by surfactants such as soap.

clues.t: Makes the top layer of a liquid act like a stretchy skin
Lets water striders walk on ponds and a carefully placed paper clip or needle rest on water
Caused by cohesion: liquid molecules pull on each other, so the ones at the top feel a net inward pull
Lowered by soap, detergents, and other surfactants
Pulls drops into spheres, the shape with the least area for their volume
Water’s value is unusually high because of hydrogen bonding: about 72 millinewtons per meter at room temperature
Measured in newtons per meter (the same as joules per square meter) and often symbolized by the Greek letter gamma
Helps drive capillary action, the climb of water up a thin tube
Water’s meniscus curves up at the glass because its adhesion to glass beats its cohesion; mercury’s curves down
Mercury’s value is much higher than water’s, so spilled mercury breaks into shiny beads
Falls as a liquid’s temperature rises
Lets you fill a glass slightly above its rim, so the water forms a dome
On the International Space Station, floating blobs of water pull themselves into balls
A substance coating the lungs’ alveoli lowers it so the tiny air sacs do not collapse
Young–Laplace equation: the pressure jump across a curved drop depends on it and the radius, so small bubbles have higher pressure inside
In 1805, Thomas Young related the contact angle of a drop on a solid to it
Marangoni effect: liquid flows from where it is low to where it is high, so soap behind a toy boat makes it zoom forward
Jurin’s law: the height a liquid climbs in a thin tube is inversely proportional to the tube’s radius
Measured with tensiometers such as a du Noüy ring or a Wilhelmy plate
In a classic classroom experiment, students count how many drops of water fit on a penny before the bulging dome of water spills
Agnes Pockels measured it with a homemade trough in her kitchen; Lord Rayleigh helped publish her work in _Nature_ in 1891
Joseph Plateau: stable soap films meet in threes at 120 degrees; it also breaks a thin falling stream into droplets
Ripples shorter than about 2 centimeters are capillary waves, flattened mainly by it rather than by gravity
Pulls a soap bubble into a sphere, the shape that encloses its air with the least area of film
Soap and detergent molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail, so they crowd onto the top of water and lower it
Holds a hanging drop onto a faucet or eyedropper until the drop’s weight grows too large
Keeps small raindrops nearly spherical; large raindrops get flattened by air resistance into a hamburger-bun shape
The “Cheerios effect”: floating bits of cereal clump together because of it and buoyancy

trap.title: Not capillary action!
trap.body: Capillary action, cohesion, adhesion, and the meniscus show up in the same clues, but each is a different answer. Cohesion is the pull between like molecules that causes this property. Capillary action is a liquid climbing a thin tube or a paper towel, which this property helps drive, and the meniscus is the curved top of a liquid in a tube.
trap.fix: A liquid acting like a skin, insects standing on water, round drops, soap lowering a value in newtons per meter, or the Greek letter gamma all mean this answer. Liquid climbing a narrow tube on its own is capillary action, and thick, slow pouring is viscosity. If you only say “tension,” expect a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Surface tension (prompt on tension; do not accept “capillary action” or “cohesion”)

topics.name: Radio waves
topics.kicker: Longest waves of the spectrum · Carry AM and FM broadcasts
topics.dates: First made and detected by Heinrich Hertz in the late 1880s
topics.briefing: Radio waves are the longest waves of the electromagnetic spectrum: some stretch longer than a football field, and all of them travel at the speed of light. Heinrich Hertz first made and detected them in a lab in the late 1880s, and Guglielmo Marconi soon used them to send messages across the Atlantic without wires. They carry AM and FM music, and giant dish telescopes collect them from pulsars and distant galaxies.
topics.answerHtml: Radio waves (accept radio radiation or radio frequencies; prompt on electromagnetic waves; do not accept “microwaves”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Karl Jansky, an engineer at Bell Labs, traced a mysterious hiss to these waves coming from the center of the Milky Way, and a unit used by astronomers is named for him. Grote Reber later built a backyard dish in Illinois to map these waves from space.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves with the longest wavelengths, used by AM and FM stations.

tossups.p: Heinrich Hertz used a spark-gap transmitter and a loop of wire to make and detect these waves in the late 1880s, proving a prediction of James Clerk Maxwell. Hertz showed they could be reflected and polarized just like light.
tossups.r: Guglielmo Marconi used them to send wireless messages. For 10 points, name these long-wavelength electromagnetic waves that carry AM and FM broadcasts.

tossups.p: Oliver Heaviside and Arthur Kennelly proposed a reflecting layer in the upper atmosphere to explain how these waves could travel past the horizon. Guglielmo Marconi had reported hearing three dots, the Morse code letter S, sent across the Atlantic on these waves in 1901.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves with the longest wavelengths, which carry AM and FM broadcasts.

tossups.p: Edward Appleton won the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physics for probing the ionosphere, a layer of charged gas that bounces some of these waves back toward the ground. That bouncing lets AM stations be heard hundreds of miles away at night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these lowest-frequency electromagnetic waves, which also carry FM and TV signals.

tossups.p: Hydrogen atoms in space give off these waves at a wavelength of 21 centimeters when an electron flips its spin, letting astronomers map the spiral arms of the Milky Way. Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered pulsars in 1967 by studying these waves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves, collected from space by giant dish telescopes.

tossups.p: Jerry Ehman circled a burst of these waves on a computer printout and wrote “Wow!” beside it in 1977. Astronomers searching for intelligent life scan the sky for these waves, and in 1974 the Arecibo telescope beamed a message on them toward the star cluster M13.
tossups.r: They carry AM and FM broadcasts. For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves, which have the longest wavelengths of all.

tossups.p: Edwin Howard Armstrong invented a way of sending sound on these waves by changing their frequency, which resisted static from lightning better than the older method of changing their amplitude. In the United States, stations using his method broadcast between 88 and 108 megahertz.
tossups.r: Antennas on cars pick them up. For 10 points, name these long-wavelength electromagnetic waves used by AM and FM stations.

tossups.p: In 1955, Bernard Burke and Kenneth Franklin discovered that Jupiter gives off strong bursts of these waves, and the moon Io affects when the bursts occur. Very low frequency versions of these waves can send messages to submerged submarines because they travel some distance into seawater.
tossups.r: They carry AM and FM broadcasts. For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves, which have longer wavelengths than microwaves.

tossups.p: Early receivers for these waves used a coherer, a glass tube of metal filings developed by Édouard Branly [“brahn-LEE”]. Russia marks May 7 as a holiday honoring Alexander Popov, who demonstrated a receiver for these waves on that day in 1895.
tossups.r: Guglielmo Marconi used them for wireless telegraphy. For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves with the longest wavelengths.

tossups.p: A half-wave dipole antenna for these waves is about half their wavelength long, so one tuned to 100 megahertz is roughly 1.5 meters long. MRI machines send pulses of these waves into the body to flip the spins of hydrogen nuclei lined up by a strong magnet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves with the lowest frequencies, used for AM and FM broadcasting.

tossups.p: Quasars got their name because astronomers first found them as starlike objects that were strong sources of these waves. The Very Large Array in New Mexico links 27 dish antennas to study the sky using these waves.
tossups.r: AM stations broadcast them at frequencies measured in kilohertz. For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves with the longest wavelengths.

tossups.p: In 1920, station KDKA in Pittsburgh used these waves to announce the results of the presidential election between Warren Harding and James Cox. Eight years earlier, wireless operators on the sinking _Titanic_ used these waves to call for help.
tossups.r: Franklin Roosevelt’s “fireside chats” reached Americans through them. For 10 points, name these long-wavelength electromagnetic waves, which also carry FM music stations.

tossups.p: At a frequency of 1 megahertz, these waves have a wavelength of about 300 meters, the speed of light divided by the frequency, which is far longer than a football field. On the electromagnetic spectrum, these waves sit just past microwaves, on the opposite end from gamma rays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves with the lowest frequencies, which carry AM and FM broadcasts.

tossups.p: A large “quiet zone” around the Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia restricts devices that give off these waves, so the telescope can detect faint signals from space. In China, a 500-meter dish called FAST collects these waves from pulsars and galaxies.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these long-wavelength electromagnetic waves, which also carry AM and FM broadcasts.

tossups.p: During World War II, a chain of British stations called Chain Home, developed under Robert Watson-Watt, bounced these waves off incoming aircraft to detect them. Walkie-talkies, garage-door openers, and baby monitors all send signals on these waves.
tossups.r: They travel at the speed of light. For 10 points, name these electromagnetic waves with the longest wavelengths, used by AM and FM stations.
