trap.title: Microwaves or these?
trap.body: Microwaves sit right next to these waves on the electromagnetic spectrum, and some engineers even count microwaves as a high-frequency kind of them, so the clues can overlap. Quiz bowl usually treats them as separate answers: microwave ovens and the cosmic microwave background mean microwaves. A bare “waves” or “electromagnetic waves” is too general and only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: AM and FM, Marconi, Hertz’s spark gap, Karl Jansky, the 21-centimeter line, pulsars, and giant dishes like Arecibo point to these waves. Ovens and the leftover glow of the Big Bang point to microwaves.
trap.line: Real answer line: Radio waves (accept radio radiation or radio frequencies; prompt on electromagnetic waves; do not accept “microwaves”)

topics.name: Superconductivity
topics.kicker: Zero electrical resistance in the deep cold · Makes magnets float
topics.dates: Discovered by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911
topics.briefing: Cool certain materials far enough and something amazing happens: electric current flows through them with zero resistance, and magnets can float above them. Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered superconductivity in 1911 by chilling mercury with liquid helium. Superconducting magnets run hospital MRI machines, and in 1987 scientists found a ceramic that works in inexpensive liquid nitrogen.
topics.answerHtml: Superconductivity (accept word forms such as superconductors or superconducting; do not accept “semiconductors” or “superfluidity”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes [“HAY-kuh KAH-mer-ling ON-us”] discovered this phenomenon in 1911 while cooling mercury with liquid helium to about 4 kelvins. Three years before, he had become the first person to liquefy helium, and he won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics for his low-temperature research.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state in which a material cooled below a critical temperature carries electric current with zero resistance.

tossups.p: In 1933, Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld [“OK-sen-felt”] found that materials in this state push magnetic fields out of their interiors, making them perfect diamagnets. That effect lets a small magnet float above a cold disk of such a material.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of zero electrical resistance reached by some materials at very low temperatures.

tossups.p: In the BCS theory of this phenomenon, an attraction carried by vibrations of a crystal lattice, called phonons, binds electrons into Cooper pairs. John Bardeen became the only person to win the Nobel Prize in Physics twice when he shared the 1972 prize for that theory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon in which a very cold material carries electric current with no resistance.

tossups.p: In 1986, Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller found this phenomenon in a copper oxide ceramic at about 35 kelvins, winning a Nobel Prize the next year. Physicists led by Paul Chu and Maw-Kuen Wu then found a compound of yttrium, barium, copper, and oxygen that shows this phenomenon above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
tossups.r: Materials in this state levitate magnets and carry current with no resistance. For 10 points, name this low-temperature phenomenon.

tossups.p: Brian Josephson predicted that pairs of electrons can tunnel through a thin insulating barrier sandwiched between two materials in this state. Devices called SQUIDs use such junctions to measure extremely weak magnetic fields, like those made by the human brain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon of zero electrical resistance, first seen in mercury in 1911.

tossups.p: Alexei Abrikosov showed that in “Type II” materials of this kind, magnetic field lines can thread through in tiny whirlpools of current called vortices. “Type I” materials lose this property all at once when the outside magnetic field passes a single critical value.
tossups.r: Materials in this state can levitate magnets. For 10 points, name this state of zero electrical resistance and perfect diamagnetism.

tossups.p: A giant particle accelerator being built in Texas, named for this phenomenon because its magnets would rely on it, was canceled by Congress in 1993. Lead shows this phenomenon below about 7 kelvins, but copper, silver, and gold are not known to show it at all.
tossups.r: In the Meissner effect, materials in this state push out magnetic fields. For 10 points, name this state in which electrical resistance drops to zero.

tossups.p: Japan’s L0 Series maglev train, which reached 603 kilometers per hour in 2015, floats above its guideway using onboard magnets made of coils in this state. The Large Hadron Collider bends beams of protons with magnets that rely on this state, which requires cooling them close to absolute zero.
tossups.r: Hospital MRI machines also use magnets in this state. For 10 points, name this phenomenon in which certain cold materials have zero electrical resistance.

tossups.p: Among pure elements at normal pressure, niobium shows this phenomenon at the highest temperature, about 9 kelvins. In 2001, Japanese researchers found that magnesium diboride, a simple compound, shows this phenomenon at 39 kelvins.
tossups.r: Magnets can float above materials in this state. For 10 points, name this phenomenon of zero electrical resistance at very low temperatures.

tossups.p: The magnetic flux through a ring in this state comes in multiples of a quantum with 2e in its denominator, a clue that electrons travel in pairs. A current set flowing around such a ring can keep circulating for years with no battery attached.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of zero electrical resistance, found in mercury by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes.

tossups.p: In 1950, experiments showed that mercury made of heavier isotopes reaches this state at a slightly lower temperature, a clue that vibrations of the crystal lattice are involved. Below the critical temperature, the electrons in such materials form pairs named for Leon Cooper.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon in which a cold material carries electric current with no resistance at all.

tossups.p: In “quantum locking” demonstrations, a thin disk in this state stays frozen in place above or even below a magnetic track because magnetic flux gets pinned inside it. The disk is usually a copper-oxide ceramic cooled with liquid nitrogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state, discovered in 1911, in which a material has zero electrical resistance.

tossups.p: The giant magnets of the ITER fusion project in France use niobium-based wires in this state. Strong enough magnetic fields or currents destroy this state, so magnet designers must stay below a critical field and a critical current.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of zero electrical resistance, reached by cooling certain materials below a critical temperature.

tossups.p: In 2015, researchers reported that hydrogen sulfide squeezed to enormous pressures reaches this state at about 203 kelvins, a record at the time. Physicists hope to find a material that shows this phenomenon at room temperature and ordinary pressure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state in which electric current flows through a material with zero resistance.

tossups.p: A packed 1987 meeting in New York City, where physicists rushed to report new copper-oxide materials showing this phenomenon, was nicknamed the “Woodstock of physics.” Classroom demonstrations often cool a ceramic disk with liquid nitrogen until a magnet floats above it, showing the Meissner effect.
tossups.r: Bardeen, Cooper, and Schrieffer explained it for ordinary metals in 1957. For 10 points, name this state in which a material loses all electrical resistance.

clues.t: Zero electrical resistance in a material cooled below its critical temperature
Materials in this state push out magnetic fields, so a magnet can float above them
Needs very low temperatures, reached with liquid helium or liquid nitrogen
Used in the magnets of MRI machines, maglev trains, and the Large Hadron Collider
Discovered in mercury in 1911 by Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, who had liquefied helium in 1908 (Nobel Prize 1913)
Meissner effect (1933, with Robert Ochsenfeld): magnetic fields are pushed out, making a perfect diamagnet
BCS theory (1957), by John Bardeen, Leon Cooper, and John Robert Schrieffer
Electrons form Cooper pairs, bound together with help from lattice vibrations called phonons
John Bardeen shared the 1972 Nobel Prize for BCS theory, making him the only person with two Nobel Prizes in Physics
1986: Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller found it in a copper oxide (cuprate) ceramic at about 35 K; Nobel Prize 1987
YBCO (yttrium barium copper oxide), found by teams led by Paul Chu and Maw-Kuen Wu, works above liquid nitrogen’s 77 K boiling point
Type I materials lose it above a single critical field; Type II materials let magnetic flux in through vortices
Josephson effect: electron pairs tunnel through a thin insulating barrier; SQUIDs use these junctions to measure tiny magnetic fields
Alexei Abrikosov explained the vortices in Type II materials (Nobel Prize 2003)
A giant particle accelerator being built in Texas, named for it because of its magnets, was canceled by Congress in 1993
Lead shows it below about 7 K, but copper, silver, and gold, the best ordinary conductors, are not known to show it
Magnetic flux through a ring comes in multiples of h over 2e, a clue that electrons travel in pairs
A persistent current in a ring can circulate for years with no battery attached
Isotope effect (1950): mercury made of heavier isotopes reaches it at a lower temperature, so lattice vibrations matter
Niobium reaches it at the highest temperature of any element at normal pressure, about 9 K
Magnesium diboride, found in 2001 by Japanese researchers, reaches it at 39 K
Flux pinning (“quantum locking”) holds a cold disk frozen in place above or even below a magnetic track
The ITER fusion project in France and Japan’s L0 Series maglev (603 km/h in 2015) both use magnets in this state
Hydrogen sulfide squeezed to enormous pressures reached it at about 203 K in 2015, a record at the time
A packed 1987 New York meeting on new copper-oxide versions of it was nicknamed the “Woodstock of physics”

trap.title: Not semiconductors or superfluids
trap.body: Semiconductors, like the silicon in computer chips, have a resistance between that of metals and insulators, and they are a different answer. Superfluidity is a cousin phenomenon in which very cold liquid helium flows with no viscosity at all. The Meissner effect is only one feature of this state, so naming it instead of the whole phenomenon is wrong.
trap.fix: Zero electrical resistance, Cooper pairs, Kamerlingh Onnes, BCS theory, or levitating magnets mean this answer. Silicon chips and transistors mean semiconductors, and frictionless liquid helium creeping up the walls of its container means superfluidity.
trap.line: Real answer line: Superconductivity (accept word forms such as superconductors; do not accept “semiconductors” or “superfluidity”)

topics.name: Capacitors
topics.kicker: Charge-storing circuit parts · Their key quantity is measured in farads
topics.briefing: A capacitor is a circuit part that stores electric charge on two metal plates kept apart by an insulator. How much charge it holds for each volt is its capacitance, measured in farads after Michael Faraday. Capacitors can dump their energy in a split second, which is why camera flashes use them, and the first one, the Leyden jar, was invented in the 1740s.
topics.answerHtml: Capacitors (accept condensers; prompt on capacitance; do not accept “resistors,” “inductors,” or “batteries”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ewald von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek [“MUSS-en-brook”] independently invented an early type of these devices in the 1740s, and the Dutch city where van Musschenbroek worked gave that version its name. Benjamin Franklin called a row of those linked jars a “battery.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices that store electric charge on two plates separated by an insulator, whose key property is measured in farads.

tossups.p: The “displacement current” that James Clerk Maxwell added to Ampère’s law accounts for the magnetic field in the gap of one of these devices while it charges. The electric field between the plates of an empty one of these devices equals the charge per area divided by the permittivity of free space.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these circuit elements that store energy in an electric field, often between two parallel plates.

tossups.p: The energy stored in one of these devices equals one-half times C times V squared. Camera flashes and defibrillators use these devices because they can dump their stored energy in a fraction of a second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices, made of two conducting plates separated by an insulator, that store electric charge.

tossups.p: When one of these devices charges through a resistor, the time constant R C is how long it takes to reach about 63 percent of the final voltage. Adding a slab of dielectric material between the plates of one of these devices raises how much charge it holds at a given voltage.
tossups.r: Their ability to store charge is measured in farads. For 10 points, name these devices that store charge on two plates.

tossups.p: Connected in parallel, the key values of these devices simply add, but in series their reciprocals add, the opposite of how resistors combine. Two identical ones wired in series have half the key value of either one alone.
tossups.r: They store charge on two plates separated by an insulator. For 10 points, name these electric circuit components rated in farads.

tossups.p: Paired with an inductor, one of these devices forms a circuit that oscillates at one over two pi times the square root of L C. Turning the tuning knob on an old radio rotated meshing metal plates in a variable version of these devices.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices that store charge and energy in an electric field between two plates.

tossups.p: The reactance of these devices equals one over two pi times frequency times C, so they block steady direct current but let alternating current pass. In the memory aid “ELI the ICE man,” the C stands for these devices, in which current leads voltage by 90 degrees.
tossups.r: They hold charge on two plates. For 10 points, name these circuit elements whose key property is measured in farads.

tossups.p: Each bit of DRAM computer memory is stored as charge on a tiny one of these devices, which leaks away unless the chip refreshes it many times a second. One of these devices placed across a power supply’s output smooths out ripples in the voltage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these electronic components that store charge on two plates separated by a dielectric.

tossups.p: Electrolytic versions of these devices use an extremely thin oxide layer on aluminum or tantalum as the insulator, so they must be connected with the correct polarity. Other versions use thin sheets of ceramic or mica between their plates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices rated in microfarads or picofarads, which store electric charge.

tossups.p: Electric double-layer versions of these components store charge in the thin Helmholtz layer where an electrode meets an electrolyte, giving them huge values of their key property. Like other types, they charge and discharge far faster than batteries but store less energy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices that store energy in an electric field, often between two parallel plates.

tossups.p: Even a lone metal sphere acts as one of these devices, storing an amount of charge per volt equal to four pi times the permittivity of free space times its radius. For one of these devices made of two parallel plates, the charge stored per volt equals the permittivity times the plate area divided by the gap.
tossups.r: Sliding a dielectric between the plates lets one hold more charge at the same voltage. For 10 points, name these devices rated in farads.

tossups.p: Most smartphone touchscreens find your finger by sensing how it disturbs a grid of tiny ones of these devices formed by crisscrossing electrodes under the glass. Dividing the charge on one of these devices by the voltage across it gives a value measured in farads.
tossups.r: That unit is named for Michael Faraday. For 10 points, name these devices that store charge on two plates separated by an insulator.

tossups.p: If the voltage across one of these devices gets too high, its insulating layer can suffer dielectric breakdown and let a spark jump between the plates. A thundercloud and the ground below it act like a giant one of these devices, with air as the insulator.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices that store charge on two plates separated by an insulator.

tossups.p: One kind of studio microphone works because sound shakes a thin diaphragm that forms one plate of these devices, so the changing gap turns sound into an electrical signal. When one of these devices is charged, its two plates hold equal and opposite amounts of charge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices, rated in farads, that store energy in an electric field.

tossups.p: A resistor and one of these devices form a simple high-pass filter, since this device lets high-frequency signals through more easily than low ones. On a circuit diagram, one of these devices is drawn as two short parallel lines with a gap between them.
tossups.r: They are rated in farads. For 10 points, name these devices that store electric charge on two plates.

clues.t: Two conducting plates separated by an insulator, used to store electric charge and energy
Rated in farads, a unit named for Michael Faraday
Store energy in the electric field between their plates
Camera flashes and defibrillators use them to release stored energy in an instant
Their key quantity, symbolized C, equals charge divided by voltage (Q = C V)
The stored energy equals one-half C V squared
A dielectric between the plates raises the key value by a factor called the dielectric constant
For parallel plates, the key value equals the permittivity times the plate area divided by the gap
In parallel their values add; in series their reciprocals add, the opposite of resistors
With a resistor, the time constant R C is the time to reach about 63 percent of full charge
The Leyden jar, invented in the 1740s, was an early type
Block steady direct current but let alternating current pass
Ewald von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek independently invented the Leyden jar; Benjamin Franklin called linked jars a “battery”
Maxwell’s displacement current explains the magnetic field in the gap while one charges
The field between empty parallel plates equals the charge per area divided by the permittivity of free space
With an inductor, forms an LC circuit that oscillates at one over two pi root L C; variable ones tuned old radios
Reactance equals one over two pi f C, so it falls as frequency rises
In the memory aid “ELI the ICE man,” the C stands for these: current leads voltage by 90 degrees
Each bit of DRAM memory is charge on a tiny one that must be refreshed; one across a power supply smooths out ripples
Electrolytic types use a thin oxide layer on aluminum or tantalum and must be connected with the correct polarity
Electric double-layer types store charge in the Helmholtz layer where an electrode meets an electrolyte
Even a lone metal sphere acts as one, storing four pi times the permittivity of free space times its radius in charge per volt
Most smartphone touchscreens sense a finger by how it disturbs a grid of tiny ones formed by crisscrossing electrodes
Too much voltage causes dielectric breakdown, letting a spark jump between the plates
In one kind of studio microphone, sound moves a thin diaphragm that is one of the plates
With a resistor it makes a high-pass filter; on circuit diagrams it is drawn as two short parallel lines

trap.title: Device or quantity?
trap.body: Every tossup on this page asks for the device, so naming its key quantity, capacitance, earns only a prompt here. In a real match, listen for the noun: “these devices” or “these circuit elements” wants capacitors, but “this quantity, measured in farads” wants capacitance, and naming the wrong one can be ruled incorrect. Players also mix them up with resistors, inductors, and batteries, which show up in the same circuit questions.
trap.fix: Plates, dielectrics, Leyden jars, and stored charge mean capacitor; a giveaway that asks for “this quantity,” the charge stored per volt, wants capacitance. Coils and henries mean inductors, ohms mean resistors, and chemical reactions that push current mean batteries.

topics.name: Galileo Galilei
topics.kicker: Italian scientist with the telescope · Jupiter’s moons and a famous trial
topics.briefing: Starting in 1609, Galileo Galilei pointed his homemade telescopes at the night sky and found mountains on the Moon, the phases of Venus, and four moons circling Jupiter. He also rolled balls down ramps to work out how objects fall, laying groundwork for Isaac Newton. Because he defended Copernicus’s idea that Earth moves around the Sun, the Roman Inquisition put him on trial in 1633 and kept him under house arrest for the rest of his life.
topics.answerHtml: Galileo Galilei (accept Galilei; do not accept “Vincenzo Galilei,” his father)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This scientist recorded Neptune in his notes in 1612 and 1613 but mistook it for a fixed star. When he looked at Saturn, his telescope could not show its rings, so he described the planet as three bodies, a large one with a smaller companion on each side.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian astronomer who discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter in 1610.

tossups.p: This scientist’s 1610 book _Sidereus Nuncius_ [“sih-DEER-ee-us NUN-see-us”], or _Starry Messenger_, reported mountains and craters on the Moon and showed that the Milky Way is made of countless stars. In that book, he named four new objects the “Medicean Stars” to honor the ruling family of Florence.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian astronomer who discovered the largest moons of Jupiter and was later tried by the Inquisition.

tossups.p: In this scientist’s 1632 _Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems_, a character named Simplicio defends the old Earth-centered view against Salviati, who speaks for the author. Simplicio also repeats an argument made by Pope Urban VIII, which angered the pope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian scientist, sentenced to house arrest in 1633 for supporting the idea that Earth moves around the Sun.

tossups.p: In a 1638 book written under house arrest and printed in the Netherlands, this scientist explained why a giant animal would need proportionally thicker bones, an idea known as the square-cube law. That book, _Two New Sciences_, also showed that a thrown object follows a parabola.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian physicist who studied falling bodies and was tried by the Roman Inquisition.

tossups.p: A paradox named for this man notes that there seem to be as many perfect squares as there are counting numbers, even though most counting numbers are not squares. This man also tried to measure the speed of light by uncovering lanterns on distant hills, but the light was too fast to time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this scientist who supported Copernicus and was sentenced to house arrest after a trial in 1633.

tossups.p: This scientist rolled balls down gently sloping ramps to slow their fall, finding that the distance traveled grows with the square of the time. He concluded that a ball rolling on a level surface would keep moving unless something stopped it, an early form of the idea of inertia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian physicist who supposedly dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

tossups.p: This man’s father was a lute player and music theorist. A story told by this man’s student Vincenzo Viviani [“vee-VYAH-nee”] says this man noticed that a swinging lamp in Pisa’s cathedral took the same time for each swing, whether the swing was wide or narrow.
tossups.r: He built his own telescope in 1609. For 10 points, name this Italian scientist who studied pendulums and falling objects.

tossups.p: This scientist argued with the Jesuit Christoph Scheiner [“SHY-ner”] over who first saw sunspots and what they were. This man’s observation that Venus goes through a full set of phases like the Moon was strong evidence against Ptolemy’s Earth-centered model.
tossups.r: He discovered four moons of Jupiter in 1610. For 10 points, name this Italian astronomer who championed the Copernican system.

tossups.p: In 1992, after a commission studied this scientist’s case, Pope John Paul II acknowledged that errors had been made in condemning him. This man is buried in Florence’s Basilica of Santa Croce, near the tomb of Michelangelo.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian scientist who was tried by the Inquisition in 1633 for supporting heliocentrism.

tossups.p: Bertolt Brecht wrote a play about this scientist’s life, and a NASA probe named for him orbited Jupiter from 1995 to 2003. The four largest moons of Jupiter are known as a group by this man’s name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian astronomer who discovered those moons in 1610 with a telescope he built himself.

tossups.p: In _The Assayer_, this scientist argued with Orazio Grassi about comets and wrote that the book of nature is written in the language of mathematics. He wrongly argued that the tides were caused by Earth’s motions, using them as proof that Earth moves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian scientist who supported the Copernican model and was tried in 1633.

tossups.p: Johannes Kepler wrote a reply welcoming this man’s 1610 discoveries, and Simon Marius later gave the moons this man discovered the names Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. This man was the first to report seeing those moons through a telescope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian astronomer, who was later put on trial by the Roman Inquisition.

tossups.p: In 1616, Cardinal Robert Bellarmine warned this man not to hold or defend the idea that Earth moves, and Copernicus’s book was suspended until corrected. Seventeen years later, this man was forced to take back his views and spent the rest of his life under house arrest near Florence.
tossups.r: He also studied falling bodies and pendulums. For 10 points, name this Italian scientist who discovered Jupiter’s four largest moons.

tossups.p: Letters to this man from his eldest daughter, a nun known as Sister Maria Celeste, were the basis of a 1999 book by Dava Sobel. According to a legend, after being forced to take back his claim that Earth moves, this man muttered “And yet it moves.”
tossups.r: This man was born in Pisa in 1564. For 10 points, name this Italian scientist who used a telescope to discover four moons of Jupiter.

tossups.p: A unit of acceleration used in gravity surveys, equal to one centimeter per second squared, is named for this man. In a thought experiment, he argued that a person in a closed cabin below the deck of a smoothly sailing ship could not tell that the ship was moving.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian scientist, the subject of a famous 1633 trial before the Inquisition.

clues.t: Discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter in 1610: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto
Built his own telescope in 1609 and turned it on the night sky
Tried by the Roman Inquisition in 1633 and kept under house arrest for supporting heliocentrism
Supported Copernicus’s idea that Earth moves around the Sun
Supposedly dropped two balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to show they fall together
_Sidereus Nuncius_ (_Starry Messenger_, 1610): mountains on the Moon and a Milky Way made of countless stars
Named Jupiter’s moons the “Medicean Stars” to honor the Medici family of Florence
Saw that Venus goes through a full set of phases like the Moon, evidence against Ptolemy’s system
_Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems_ (1632): Simplicio vs. Salviati; Pope Urban VIII was angered when Simplicio repeated his argument
Rolled balls down ramps (inclined planes): the distance fallen grows with the square of the time
A ball on a level surface would keep rolling unless stopped: an early form of the idea of inertia
A story told by his student Vincenzo Viviani says a swinging lamp in Pisa’s cathedral led him to study pendulums
Legend says he muttered “And yet it moves” after being forced to take back his views
Born in Pisa in 1564, the same year as William Shakespeare; later taught at Padua
Recorded Neptune in 1612 and 1613 but mistook it for a fixed star
His telescope could not show Saturn’s rings, so Saturn looked like three bodies, a large one with a companion on each side
_Two New Sciences_ (1638), printed in the Netherlands: the square-cube law and the parabolic path of a thrown object
His paradox: there seem to be as many perfect squares as counting numbers; he also tried to time light with lanterns on distant hills
His father, Vincenzo, was a lute player and music theorist
Argued with the Jesuit Christoph Scheiner about who first saw sunspots and what they were
_The Assayer_: argued with Orazio Grassi about comets and wrote that nature is written in the language of mathematics
Wrongly argued that Earth’s motions cause the tides, as proof that Earth moves
Johannes Kepler welcomed his 1610 discoveries; Simon Marius gave the four moons their names
1616: Cardinal Robert Bellarmine warned him not to hold or defend the idea that Earth moves
In 1992, Pope John Paul II acknowledged that errors had been made in condemning him; he is buried in Santa Croce in Florence
Subject of a Bertolt Brecht play; a NASA probe named for him orbited Jupiter from 1995 to 2003
His eldest daughter, the nun Sister Maria Celeste, wrote him letters used in Dava Sobel’s 1999 book
The gal, a unit of acceleration, is named for him; his closed-ship-cabin thought experiment shows that steady motion cannot be felt

trap.title: Copernicus, Kepler, or him?
trap.body: Copernicus (the Polish astronomer who published the Sun-centered model in 1543), Johannes Kepler (who found that planets move in ellipses), and this man all show up in questions about heliocentrism. Tycho Brahe, Kepler’s mentor, made the best measurements of the sky without a telescope. Isaac Newton came later and built his laws of motion on this man’s work.
trap.fix: A telescope, Jupiter’s moons, Venus’s phases, sunspots, falling bodies, pendulums, the Inquisition, or house arrest point to this man. Ellipses and three laws of planetary motion mean Kepler, and _De revolutionibus_ or 1543 means Copernicus.

topics.name: Enrico Fermi
topics.kicker: Builder of the first nuclear reactor · 1938 Nobel for slow neutrons
topics.briefing: Enrico Fermi was an Italian physicist who was brilliant at both theory and experiments. He won the 1938 Nobel Prize for making elements radioactive with slow neutrons, then left Fascist Italy for the United States, where his team built Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor, in 1942. Element 100, fermium, is named for him, and so are the particles called fermions.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This physicist found that neutrons slowed down by passing through paraffin wax were far better at making elements radioactive. He won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for that work, then used the trip to Stockholm to move his family to the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian-American physicist who led the team that built the first nuclear reactor in Chicago in 1942.

tossups.p: After this scientist’s team succeeded, Arthur Compton telephoned James Conant with the coded message “The Italian navigator has landed in the New World.” That success came on December 2, 1942, under the stands of a football field at the University of Chicago.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who led the building of Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor.

tossups.p: The journal _Nature_ turned down this physicist’s 1933 theory of beta decay as too far removed from reality. In that theory, which first described the weak force, this man used the name “neutrino,” or “little neutral one,” for a particle proposed by Wolfgang Pauli.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian physicist who won the 1938 Nobel Prize and later worked on the Manhattan Project.

tossups.p: During a 1950 lunchtime conversation at Los Alamos about flying saucers, this physicist asked a question usually quoted as “Where is everybody?” A paradox named for him asks why, if the galaxy is so old and so large, no signs of alien civilizations have been found.
tossups.r: He won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics. For 10 points, name this Italian-born physicist whose team achieved the first controlled nuclear chain reaction.

tossups.p: At the first atomic bomb test in 1945, this physicist estimated the blast’s strength by dropping scraps of paper and watching how far they were blown. He loved quick estimation puzzles, like how many piano tuners live in Chicago, and such puzzles are named for him.
tossups.r: He was born in Rome in 1901. For 10 points, name this Italian-American physicist who led the team that built Chicago Pile-1.

tossups.p: In a metal at absolute zero, the highest energy level that electrons fill is named for this physicist. Particles that obey the Pauli exclusion principle, such as electrons, protons, and neutrons, are also named for him, and statistics named for him and Paul Dirac describe how such particles fill energy levels.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who led the first controlled nuclear chain reaction and won the 1938 Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: In 1934, this physicist’s team bombarded uranium with neutrons and believed they had made new elements heavier than uranium, even proposing names for two of them. Ida Noddack suggested instead that the uranium nuclei had split, an idea later confirmed as nuclear fission.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian physicist whose team later built the first nuclear reactor under a stadium in Chicago.

tossups.p: Emilio Segrè belonged to this physicist’s group of young researchers in Rome, nicknamed the “Via Panisperna boys” after the street where their institute stood. Colleagues jokingly called this man “the Pope” because he never seemed to be wrong about physics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian physicist who later moved to the United States and worked on the Manhattan Project.

tossups.p: Element 100, first found in the debris of a 1952 hydrogen bomb test, is named for this scientist. A particle physics laboratory in Batavia, Illinois, and a NASA gamma-ray space telescope launched in 2008 are also named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who led the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in 1942.

tossups.p: This man’s wife, Laura, wrote the memoir _Atoms in the Family_ about their life together. Because Laura was Jewish, Italy’s 1938 racial laws pushed the family to leave Fascist Italy for the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian-born physicist who won the 1938 Nobel Prize and built the first nuclear reactor.

tossups.p: A “golden rule” named for this physicist gives the rate at which a quantum system jumps from one state to another. A unit of length used for atomic nuclei, equal to one femtometer, is also nicknamed for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this physicist who led the team that built Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor.

tossups.p: George Weil slowly pulled out the last control rod of a reactor while this physicist checked the readings with a slide rule. That reactor was a stack of graphite blocks and uranium, controlled by cadmium rods that soak up neutrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian physicist whose team built Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor, in 1942.

tossups.p: This physicist studied at the Scuola Normale Superiore [“SKWOH-lah nor-MAH-leh soo-peh-RYOH-reh”] in Pisa before becoming a professor in Rome. Soon after he moved to Columbia University in 1939, his group helped show that uranium nuclei give off extra neutrons when they split, which made a chain reaction seem possible.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian physicist who won the 1938 Nobel Prize for work with slow neutrons.

tossups.p: In 1944, this physicist helped start up the B Reactor at Hanford, Washington, the first large reactor built to make plutonium. Earlier, he had moved from Columbia University to the University of Chicago to work on the Manhattan Project.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Italian-American physicist who was born in Rome and won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics.

tossups.p: This physicist and Leo Szilard [“SIL-ard”] shared a patent for a “neutronic reactor.” Years earlier in Rome, this man had found that neutrons slowed down by water or paraffin wax were much better at making elements radioactive.
tossups.r: He gave the neutrino its name. For 10 points, name this Italian-born physicist who achieved the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in Chicago.

Won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for making new radioactive substances with neutrons

Worked on the Manhattan Project, which built the first atomic bombs
Found that neutrons slowed by paraffin wax or water are far better at making elements radioactive

Particles that obey the Pauli exclusion principle, like electrons, protons, and neutrons, are named for him
Element 100, a particle physics lab in Batavia, Illinois, and a 2008 NASA gamma-ray telescope are named for him
Gave the neutrino (“little neutral one”) its name; Wolfgang Pauli had proposed the particle
His 1933 theory of beta decay first described the weak force; the journal _Nature_ rejected it as too far from reality
At the first atomic bomb test (1945), estimated the blast’s strength from how far falling scraps of paper were blown
Statistics named for him and Paul Dirac describe how such particles fill energy levels
In a metal at absolute zero, the highest energy level filled by electrons is named for him
1934: his team thought it had made elements heavier than uranium; Ida Noddack suggested the nuclei had split (fission)
Led the “Via Panisperna boys” in Rome, a group of young physicists that included Emilio Segrè
Colleagues jokingly called him “the Pope” because he never seemed to be wrong about physics
A “golden rule” for how fast a quantum system jumps between states is named for him
The femtometer, a length unit used for atomic nuclei, is nicknamed for him
George Weil pulled the last control rod; the pile was graphite blocks and uranium, controlled with cadmium rods
His wife Laura wrote the memoir _Atoms in the Family_

trap.title: Not Oppenheimer or Szilard
trap.body: Many scientists worked on the first reactor and the Manhattan Project. J. Robert Oppenheimer directed the Los Alamos lab that designed the bomb, Leo Szilard drafted the 1939 letter Albert Einstein signed to warn President Roosevelt, and Wolfgang Pauli proposed the neutrino that this man named. Several other answer lines are also named after this man, such as fermions and fermium.
trap.fix: Chicago Pile-1, slow neutrons, the 1938 Nobel Prize, the “Italian navigator,” estimation puzzles, and naming the neutrino point to this man. If a question asks for “these particles” or “this element,” answer with the thing, not the person.

topics.name: Ferromagnetism
topics.kicker: Spins that line up on their own · Why iron makes permanent magnets
topics.briefing: Ferromagnetism is the strong magnetism of iron, nickel, and cobalt, the kind that makes permanent magnets possible. Inside these metals, the tiny magnetic spins of electrons line up on their own in small regions called domains. Heat a piece of iron past about 770 degrees Celsius, its Curie temperature, and the spins scramble, so the iron loses its strong magnetism.
topics.answerHtml: Ferromagnetism (accept word forms such as ferromagnetic; prompt on magnetism; do not accept “ferrimagnetism,” “paramagnetism,” or “antiferromagnetism”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Pierre Weiss explained this phenomenon by imagining an internal “molecular field” and by proposing that a material showing it is split into small regions called domains. Inside each domain, the spins of unpaired electrons all point the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong type of magnetic behavior shown by iron, nickel, and cobalt.

tossups.p: Above a temperature named for Pierre Curie, a material loses this property and becomes merely paramagnetic. For iron, that temperature is about 770 degrees Celsius, which is why Earth’s hot core cannot be one giant permanent magnet.
tossups.r: Its name comes from the Latin word for iron. For 10 points, name this phenomenon that lets iron, nickel, and cobalt become permanent magnets.

tossups.p: Magnetizing and demagnetizing a material with this property traces out a hysteresis loop, whose width shows the material’s coercivity. Materials with high coercivity make good permanent magnets, while “soft” ones with low coercivity are used in transformer cores.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon, the strongest kind of magnetic behavior, found in iron and nickel.

tossups.p: In the Barkhausen effect, a material with this property magnetizes in tiny jumps as the walls between its domains suddenly shift, which can be heard as clicks in a loudspeaker. Bloch walls are one kind of boundary between those domains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon in which unpaired electron spins line up on their own, as in iron magnets.

tossups.p: The Ising [“EE-sing”] model, a famous mathematical model of this phenomenon, pictures a grid of spins that can each point only up or down and that tend to line up with their neighbors. A simple compass needle is often a sliver of steel that stays magnetized because of this phenomenon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon in which neighboring electron spins line up, letting iron form permanent magnets.

tossups.p: Werner Heisenberg showed that this phenomenon comes from the exchange interaction, a quantum effect that makes it cheaper in energy for neighboring electron spins to point the same way. An iron nail held near a magnet becomes a temporary magnet that can pick up paper clips because of this phenomenon.
tossups.r: Materials with this property are strongly attracted to magnets. For 10 points, name this kind of magnetic ordering shown by iron, cobalt, and nickel.

tossups.p: James Joule found in 1842 that an iron bar changes length slightly when magnetized, as domains inside materials with this property turn to line up with the field. That effect, magnetostriction, makes the iron cores of transformers hum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that lets iron, nickel, and cobalt be strongly magnetized.

tossups.p: Louis Néel [“nay-EL”] won a Nobel Prize for studying two cousins of this phenomenon in which neighboring spins point in opposite directions. In this phenomenon itself, neighboring spins line up parallel, giving a material a large spontaneous magnetization.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong magnetic behavior of iron, which lets it become a permanent magnet.

tossups.p: Gadolinium shows this property only below about 20 degrees Celsius, close to room temperature. Alnico magnets, named for aluminum, nickel, and cobalt, and powerful neodymium magnets, made of neodymium, iron, and boron, both rely on this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of iron, nickel, and cobalt that allows permanent magnets.

tossups.p: Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physics for giant magnetoresistance, seen when very thin layers of metals with this property are separated by nonmagnetic layers. Computer hard drives store bits in tiny regions of a material with this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon that makes iron, nickel, and cobalt so strongly magnetic.

tossups.p: A liquid containing tiny magnetic particles, spread on a polished crystal, forms Bitter patterns that outline the domains of a material with this property. Stroking a steel needle with a magnet makes the needle’s domains line up, so the needle becomes a weak magnet.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong magnetic behavior, whose name comes from the Latin word for iron.

tossups.p: Above its critical temperature, a material that shows this phenomenon follows the Curie–Weiss law, with magnetic susceptibility inversely proportional to the temperature minus the critical temperature. Below that temperature, the material’s spins line up on their own in a phase transition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon that makes iron, nickel, and cobalt strongly attracted to magnets.

tossups.p: Felix Bloch described ripples of tilted spins, known as magnons, that travel through a material with this property. Bloch walls, named for him, separate the regions called domains in such a material, and heating or hammering a magnet can scramble those domains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this phenomenon in which electron spins line up to make iron a permanent magnet.

tossups.p: A material with this property can have a relative permeability in the thousands, so wrapping a wire coil around a soft iron core makes an electromagnet far stronger. Unlike paramagnetic materials, such materials can stay magnetized after the outside field is removed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strongest form of magnetic behavior, shown by iron, nickel, and cobalt.

tossups.p: When a material with this property cools below its critical temperature, its spins must all pick one direction, a classic example of spontaneous symmetry breaking. Iron, cobalt, and nickel are the best-known elements with this property.
tossups.r: A steel paper clip sticks to a magnet because of it. For 10 points, name this phenomenon that lets these metals become permanent magnets.

Lets materials become permanent magnets
Its name comes from _ferrum_, the Latin word for iron
Unpaired electron spins line up parallel to each other on their own
The strongest kind of magnetic behavior, far stronger than paramagnetism or diamagnetism
Such materials are split into small regions called domains, where all the spins point the same way
Lost above the Curie temperature (about 770 °C for iron), where the material becomes paramagnetic
Earth’s core is too hot to be a giant permanent magnet, since it is above iron’s Curie temperature

“Hard” materials with high coercivity make permanent magnets; “soft” iron is used in transformer cores
Stroking a steel needle with a magnet lines up its domains; heating or hammering a magnet can scramble them
Neodymium magnets (neodymium, iron, boron) and alnico magnets (aluminum, nickel, cobalt) rely on it

Relative permeability can be in the thousands, so a soft iron core makes an electromagnet far stronger
Barkhausen effect: magnetization changes in tiny jumps as domain walls shift, heard as clicks in a loudspeaker
Bloch walls are one kind of boundary between domains; Felix Bloch also described spin waves called magnons
The Ising model pictures it as a grid of spins that point only up or down and tend to line up with their neighbors
A simple compass needle is often a sliver of steel that stays magnetized because of it
Werner Heisenberg traced it to the quantum exchange interaction between neighboring spins
An iron nail held near a magnet becomes a temporary magnet that can pick up paper clips

trap.title: One letter makes it wrong
trap.body: Ferrimagnetism, spelled with an i, is a different answer: neighboring spins point in opposite directions but do not fully cancel, as in magnetite (lodestone) and ferrites. In antiferromagnetism the opposite spins cancel completely, paramagnetism is a weak attraction only while a field is applied, and diamagnetism is a weak push away from a magnet. Plain “magnetism” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: If all the neighboring spins line up the same way, with clues like iron, nickel, cobalt, domains, hysteresis, or a Curie temperature, say ferromagnetism, with an o. Magnetite, lodestone, and ferrites usually mean ferrimagnetism, and a Néel temperature points to antiferromagnetism.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ferromagnetism (accept ferromagnetic; prompt on magnetism; do not accept “ferrimagnetism” or “antiferromagnetism”)

topics.name: Pendulums
topics.kicker: A weight swinging from a pivot · Kept time and proved Earth spins
topics.dates: Pendulum clock invented by Christiaan Huygens, 1656
topics.briefing: A pendulum is just a weight swinging from a string or rod, but it changed the world. Galileo noticed that each swing takes about the same time, wide or narrow, and in 1656 Christiaan Huygens used that idea to invent the pendulum clock, which stayed the most accurate kind of clock until the 1930s. In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a giant pendulum in Paris to prove that Earth rotates.
topics.answerHtml: pendulums (accept specific types like Foucault pendulums or simple pendulums; prompt on oscillators)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1672, Jean Richer [“ree-SHAY”] had to shorten one of these devices in Cayenne, near the equator, to make it keep the same time it kept in Paris, a sign that gravity is slightly weaker there. The time each swing takes depends on the device’s length and on gravity, but not on its mass.
tossups.r: Christiaan Huygens invented the first clock regulated by one of these devices. For 10 points, name these swinging weights that keep time in grandfather clocks.

tossups.p: Christiaan Huygens [“HOY-gunz”] proved that one of these devices would keep perfect time if its bob moved along a curve called a cycloid, so he guided its string between curved metal “cheeks.” He described his designs in the 1673 book _Horologium Oscillatorium_.
tossups.r: For small swings, the period of one of these devices equals two pi times the square root of its length over g. For 10 points, name these swinging weights.

tossups.p: At the North Pole, the direction in which one of these devices swings would turn a full circle in about a day, but at the equator it would not turn at all. In 1851, Léon Foucault [“foo-KOH”] hung a 67-meter-long one from the dome of the Panthéon in Paris to prove that Earth rotates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these swinging devices, which Galileo studied after watching a lamp sway in a cathedral, according to a famous story.

tossups.p: Henry Kater designed a “reversible” one of these devices that could swing from either of two pivots, letting scientists measure the strength of gravity very precisely. Making one of these devices four times longer doubles the time it takes to complete each swing.
tossups.r: Galileo noticed that wide and narrow swings of these devices take about the same time. For 10 points, name these weights that hang from a pivot and swing back and forth.

tossups.p: Benjamin Robins invented a “ballistic” type of these devices that finds a bullet’s speed by measuring how high a heavy wooden block swings after the bullet lodges in it. One of these devices moves fastest at the bottom of its path and stops for an instant at the top of each swing.
tossups.r: The time each one takes per swing depends on its length but not its mass. For 10 points, name these swinging weights, which keep time in grandfather clocks.

tossups.p: Hanging one of these devices from the bottom of another creates a system famous for chaos, in which tiny changes in the starting position lead to wildly different motion. A single one of these devices follows simple harmonic motion for small swings, because the sine of a small angle almost equals the angle itself.
tossups.r: These devices keep time in grandfather clocks. For 10 points, name these devices, each made of a bob hanging from a string or rod.

tossups.p: A giant steel ball hung near the top of the Taipei 101 skyscraper acts as one of these devices, swinging to reduce the building’s sway in strong winds. Christiaan Huygens noticed that two clocks run by these devices, hung from the same beam, soon fell into a matching rhythm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these swinging weights, one of which Léon Foucault used to show that Earth rotates.

tossups.p: In the 1790s, French scientists considered defining the meter as the length of one of these devices that takes exactly one second per swing, about 99 centimeters, but they chose a fraction of the distance from the North Pole to the equator instead.
tossups.r: The time each swing takes does not depend on the mass of the bob. For 10 points, name these swinging devices, which regulate grandfather clocks.

tossups.p: Balancing a broomstick on your palm and keeping a self-balancing Segway upright are both versions of the “inverted” form of these devices. In an ordinary one of these devices, potential energy is greatest at the top of each swing, and kinetic energy is greatest at the bottom.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these devices, each a weight on a string or rod that swings back and forth from a fixed point.

tossups.p: Vincenzo Viviani [“vee-VYAH-nee”] wrote that his teacher, while still a student, used his own pulse to time a lamp swaying in the cathedral of Pisa, finding that these devices take nearly the same time per swing whether they swing wide or narrow. That property is called isochronism [“eye-SOCK-ruh-niz-um”].
tossups.r: That teacher was Galileo. For 10 points, name these swinging weights, later used by Christiaan Huygens to design accurate clocks.

tossups.p: For a “physical” or “compound” type of these devices, like a swinging rod, the period depends on its moment of inertia and on how far its center of mass sits from the pivot. On the Moon, a simple one of these devices would take about two and a half times as long per swing as on Earth.
tossups.r: Galileo and Christiaan Huygens studied these devices. For 10 points, name these swinging devices, one of which Léon Foucault used to prove that Earth rotates.

tossups.p: In the “conical” type of these devices, the bob moves in a horizontal circle, so its string traces out a cone. In an ordinary one, the restoring force pulling the bob back toward the middle equals its weight times the sine of the angle from vertical.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these swinging weights, found in grandfather clocks, whose period equals two pi times the square root of length divided by g.

tossups.p: Isaac Newton filled the hollow bobs of these devices with gold, silver, lead, glass, sand, salt, wood, water, and wheat, and found that all of them swung at the same rate. Air resistance and friction at the pivot slowly shrink the swings of real ones, an effect called damping.
tossups.r: In 1656, Christiaan Huygens used one of these devices to design a far more accurate clock. For 10 points, name these swinging devices, which keep time in grandfather clocks.

tossups.p: An invention called the anchor escapement let clocks swing these devices through much smaller arcs, which led to tall “longcase” clocks. Sliding the weight farther up the arm of a wind-up metronome slows its beat, much like lengthening one of these devices.
tossups.r: Galileo and Christiaan Huygens both studied these devices. For 10 points, name these swinging timekeepers found inside grandfather clocks.

tossups.p: Christiaan Huygens hoped that clocks run by these devices could help sailors find longitude, but the rolling of ships at sea spoiled their timekeeping. A playground swing pushed in rhythm with its natural frequency goes higher, because the swing acts as one of these devices.
tossups.r: Longer ones take more time per swing. For 10 points, name these weights hanging from a pivot, one of which Léon Foucault used to show that Earth spins.

trap.title: Pendulum or spring?
trap.body: Pendulums and masses bouncing on springs are the two classic examples of simple harmonic motion, so their clues can sound alike. For small swings, a pendulum’s period depends only on its length and gravity, while a spring’s depends on the mass and on the spring’s stiffness (Hooke’s law). Literature questions on Poe’s “The Pit and the Pendulum” or Umberto Eco’s novel _Foucault’s Pendulum_ want the title, not the device.
trap.fix: Length, a bob, a pivot, clocks, Galileo, Huygens, or Foucault means a pendulum. A spring constant, stretching, or Hooke’s law means a spring; if the question asks for “this motion,” say simple harmonic motion.
trap.line: Real answer line: pendulums (accept specific types like Foucault pendulums or simple pendulums; prompt on oscillators)
